narrative:
When the tribunal’s clerk produces the forged ledger that would condemn Mara’s oldest rival, Iven recognizes his own cipher in the margins. He does not confess that he altered the original months ago; the admission would expose the larger operation and make Mara’s execution certain. Instead, he interrupts with a dry objection: “If we are sentencing people by penmanship, we should at least hang the clerk. His handwriting is worse.” The joke earns a few uneasy laughs, but his fear shows in what he refuses to do—he will not meet Mara’s eyes, and he keeps one hand pressed over the cut in his palm where the missing seal is hidden.

Iven bargains for access to the archive, claiming he can prove the ledger was tampered with if Mara is released into his custody. The tribunal accepts because his reputation makes the offer useful, not because anyone trusts him. Mara resists the rescue, recognizing that custody could be another kind of imprisonment. She demands a price: Iven must surrender the seal and let her choose the first witness. He agrees, though doing so gives up the only evidence that could clear him.

In the archive, Mara discovers the seal wrapped in the strip of cloth from Iven’s bandage. He says he kept it because “someone had to preserve the evidence.” She answers that evidence usually survives better than people. Their exchange carries the apology neither will name: he is sorry for making her carry the consequences of his choice; she knows it and refuses to absolve him. They proceed together only because each has imposed a condition the other cannot evade. Iven’s protection costs him control of the investigation and leaves his guilt concealed. Mara is spared immediate punishment, but her distrust remains intact. She permits him to stand beside her—not as an ally, but as the debtor whose next choice will be tested.
title: The Price of Silence
